text: A logistics company wants to automate shipment exception handling. Exceptions follow a predictable sequence: classify the issue type, check inventory, calculate a resolution, and notify the customer. Volume is high (50,000/day), steps rarely change, and the company needs predictable latency and cost. Which architectural pattern best fits this use case?
options: An autonomous multi-agent system where agents negotiate the resolution path dynamically on every shipment
An augmented LLM pattern where a single Claude call with unrestricted tool access decides the entire sequence at runtime
A monolithic prompt that embeds all business rules and expects Claude to execute all four steps in one unstructured response
A fixed workflow architecture with predefined steps and deterministic control flow, calling Claude at specific stages
correct_answer: A fixed workflow architecture with predefined steps and deterministic control flow, calling Claude at specific stages
explanation: When the steps and sequence are known in advance and consistency, cost predictability, and latency control matter, a workflow pattern (orchestrated, deterministic steps with Claude invoked at specific points, option D) is the best fit. Agentic/autonomous patterns (option A) are better suited to open-ended problems requiring dynamic planning, which adds unpredictability and cost at high volume. A single augmented LLM call (option B) lacks the deterministic control flow needed for reliable, auditable multi-step processing at scale. A monolithic prompt approach (option C) sacrifices modularity, observability, and reliability.

text: A healthcare provider asks an architect to design a system where Claude drafts clinical summary notes from doctor dictations, but the use case may expand later to include scheduling, billing lookups, and insurance pre-authorization. The provider wants to start simply but avoid a costly rearchitecture later. Which decomposition approach best balances current simplicity with future extensibility?
options: Design a modular architecture where summarization is implemented as an independent capability, with clear interfaces that allow additional tools/agents to be added later without restructuring the core system
Build a single large agent today with all anticipated tools (scheduling, billing, insurance, summarization) pre-integrated, even though only summarization is needed now
Hard-code the summarization logic directly into the orchestration layer so it can be replaced wholesale when new requirements arrive
Defer all architecture decisions until the full scope of future features is confirmed by the client
correct_answer: Design a modular architecture where summarization is implemented as an independent capability, with clear interfaces that allow additional tools/agents to be added later without restructuring the core system
explanation: Sound decomposition favors building loosely coupled, modular capabilities with well-defined interfaces (option A), enabling incremental extension (e.g., adding new tools or agents) without re-architecting the core system. Pre-building unused tools (option B) introduces capability bloat and unnecessary security/maintenance surface area before it's needed. Hard-coding logic into orchestration (option C) creates tight coupling that increases future rework. Deferring all design decisions (option D) is impractical and ignores the value of incremental, extensible delivery.

text: An enterprise wants to use Claude to automate contract review, which requires reading a 60-page document, cross-referencing clauses against a legal playbook, flagging risky terms, and drafting redline suggestions. Business stakeholders need to see measurable productivity gains while maintaining consistent legal accuracy. Which approach best aligns the solution design to business value while managing architectural risk?
options: A single Claude call processing the entire document and playbook in one pass, trusting that a long context window alone guarantees accurate cross-referencing
A fully autonomous agent empowered to edit and finalize the contract without human review, to maximize turnaround speed
A decomposed pipeline that chunks the contract, retrieves relevant playbook sections per clause, and uses a feedback loop where flagged items are reviewed by legal staff before finalization
Bypassing retrieval entirely and relying on the model's general training knowledge of contract law for clause comparisons
correct_answer: A decomposed pipeline that chunks the contract, retrieves relevant playbook sections per clause, and uses a feedback loop where flagged items are reviewed by legal staff before finalization
explanation: Option C reflects end-to-end architecture best practice: decomposing the problem (chunking/clause-level processing), incorporating retrieval matched to the task, and closing the loop with human validation—aligning to both productivity (business value) and risk management (accuracy, compliance). Relying purely on long context (option A) risks accuracy issues and doesn't scale reliably. Full autonomy without human review (option B) is inappropriate given legal risk exposure. Ignoring retrieval and relying on general knowledge (option D) risks outdated or incorrect legal guidance since playbook-specific terms won't be grounded.

text: A retail company is designing a multi-agent system: one agent handles product recommendations, another manages inventory checks, and a third drafts customer-facing responses. During design review, an architect notices the three agents each independently call the same external pricing API, causing redundant calls and inconsistent prices if the API updates mid-session. What is the best orchestration fix?
options: Instruct each agent via prompt engineering to double check pricing consistency with the other two agents before responding
Introduce a shared orchestrator or coordinator pattern where pricing is fetched once and passed as shared context to all three agents
Remove the pricing API call from two of the three agents at random to reduce redundant calls
Increase the temperature setting on each agent so that minor pricing differences are less noticeable to customers
correct_answer: Introduce a shared orchestrator or coordinator pattern where pricing is fetched once and passed as shared context to all three agents
explanation: In multi-agent orchestration, a coordinator/orchestrator pattern that centralizes shared state (like a single pricing fetch, option B) prevents redundant calls and guarantees consistency across agents. Relying on agents to self-coordinate via prompting (option A) is unreliable and not a structural fix. Randomly removing calls (option C) doesn't address the root cause and may break functionality. Adjusting temperature (option D) does not address the architectural issue and could reduce output quality elsewhere.

text: A financial services firm's leadership wants to deploy a Claude-based solution for loan application review. They specify a hard requirement: 95% of reviews must complete within 3 seconds, and the system must integrate with an existing rules engine for compliance checks. The architect is choosing between an agentic pattern (Claude autonomously plans and calls tools as needed) and an augmented LLM pattern (a single Claude call with direct access to a fixed set of tools, no multi-step planning). Which factor should most heavily influence the final decision?
options: Whichever pattern uses the newest Claude model, since newer models are inherently better regardless of architecture
The agentic pattern should always be preferred for enterprise use cases because it demonstrates more advanced AI capability to stakeholders
Pattern choice is irrelevant as long as the system prompt instructs Claude to respond within three seconds
The strict low-latency SLA and compliance integration favor the augmented LLM pattern, since agentic planning introduces variable, often higher latency from iterative tool-call loops
correct_answer: The strict low-latency SLA and compliance integration favor the augmented LLM pattern, since agentic planning introduces variable, often higher latency from iterative tool-call loops
explanation: Architectural pattern selection must align to business SLAs (option D). Agentic patterns involve iterative reasoning/tool-call loops that introduce latency variability, which conflicts with a strict 95th-percentile 3-second SLA. An augmented LLM pattern (single call, fixed toolset, more deterministic) better supports predictable low latency and simpler integration with a fixed compliance rules engine. Model recency (option A) doesn't address the latency/architecture trade-off. Preferring agentic patterns for perceived sophistication (option B) ignores actual business constraints. Prompt instructions alone (option C) cannot overcome architectural latency characteristics inherent to iterative tool-calling.
